paper.title: Learning predictive latent structure from unclustered neural spike trains
paper.abstract: Neural activity patterns enable perception, thought, and action. A powerful approach to understanding these abilities involves identifying low-dimensional, interpretable latent variables that capture the relationship between activity patterns, the information they represent, and the computations they support. Yet current methods often yield variables that are difficult to interpret and require data preprocessing that limits their accuracy and temporal resolution. Here we introduce Contrastive Prediction of Point Process Observations (C3PO), an unsupervised method that learns a predictive, interpretable latent variable representation directly from continuous time neural spiking without requiring spike-sorting or binning. C3PO recovers structure associated with known latent variables across a variety of data sets without access to those variables during training. It identifies dynamics on timescales from tens of milliseconds to hours and reveals previously unreported representations and their dynamics. These results establish C3PO as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional point-process data sets.

paper.title: Structure learning and context inference emerge from next-state prediction in a cerebellar-medial temporal lobe circuit
paper.abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.

paper.title: Preparatory Bias Currents Alone Write Letters and Words in a Fixed Recurrent Circuit
paper.abstract: We show that preparatory input currents, or bias currents, alone can make a recurrent circuit with fixed weights write all 52 cursive letters, and words built from them. Each letter is produced by its own bias pattern, ramped in as a preparatory drive and withdrawn at a go cue; the recurrent weights and the readout never change, and the readout's weights are random, with a single global gain picked on four letters (a-d). We take the stability-optimized circuits (SOCs) of Hennequin et al. and extend them with mutual inhibition: all inhibitory neurons inhibit one another through a single shared weight (MISOC, mutual inhibition SOC). With 200 units, the pen of the SOC stays on average 1.7% of a letter width from the target over all 52 letters, and that of the MISOC 0.9% (25 random circuits; R2 = 0.996 and 0.999). The other 48 letters are learned through their bias patterns alone, without changing a single synapse, so new letters cannot disturb old ones. Letters learned one at a time chain into words in one continuous run. Mutual inhibition improves the circuit: with a shared weight of 0.5 the MISOC writes with 16-48% less error than the SOC at every network size tested (50 to 200 units), and with fifty network-derived input channels instead of one bias per neuron it keeps its advantage. Bias currents and mutual inhibition let small, fixed circuits hold a large and growing motor repertoire and switch within it without any synaptic change.

paper.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
paper.abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.
